questions.stem: In the sentence "The egusi soup smells delicious", the word *smells* is which kind of verb?
questions.explanation: The soup is not performing the act of smelling; the verb simply connects the subject to a word that describes it. *Delicious* is an adjective describing the soup, so *smells* is a linking verb here. Test it by substituting a form of *be*: "The soup is delicious" still makes sense, which confirms the link.

distractorRationale.a: *Smells* is an action verb in "The dog smells the meat", where the dog actually does the smelling
distractorRationale.c: Auxiliaries such as have, be and do help a main verb; here *smells* stands alone
distractorRationale.d: Modals are can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will and would

questions.stem: Identify the auxiliary verb in the sentence "The students have completed their agricultural science project."
questions.explanation: An auxiliary or helping verb works with a main verb to show tense, voice or mood. Here *have* combines with the past participle *completed* to form the present perfect tense. *Completed* carries the meaning, so it is the main verb, while *have* only helps.

distractorRationale.a: *Students* is the noun acting as subject
distractorRationale.c: *Completed* is the main verb, the one that carries the meaning
distractorRationale.d: *Project* is the noun acting as direct object

questions.stem: Write the past participle of the verb *lie*, meaning to rest in a horizontal position.
questions.explanation: The principal parts are lie, lay, lain — so the perfect tense is "the book has lain there for a week". Students confuse this with *lay* (lay, laid, laid), which means to put something down, and with *lie* meaning to tell an untruth (lie, lied, lied).

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "The messenger has already ______ the file on the director's table."
questions.explanation: The messenger put something down, so the verb needed is *lay* (lay, laid, laid), which is transitive and takes the object *the file*. After *has*, the past participle is required, giving *laid*.

distractorRationale.a: *Lain* is the participle of intransitive *lie* and cannot take an object such as *the file*
distractorRationale.c: *Lay* is the simple past form, which cannot follow the auxiliary *has*
distractorRationale.d: *Lied* belongs to *lie* meaning to tell an untruth

questions.stem: In which of the following sentences is the verb used intransitively?

options.text: The baby slept peacefully throughout the journey.
The driver repaired the punctured tyre.
Uche bought two loaves of bread.

questions.explanation: An intransitive verb needs no object to complete its meaning. Ask "slept what?" and the question makes no sense, so *slept* is intransitive; *peacefully* is an adverb, not an object. In the other three sentences you can ask "repaired what?", "explained what?" and "bought what?" and get an answer.

distractorRationale.d: *Bought* takes the object *two loaves of bread*

questions.stem: In the sentence "The choir sang the anthem beautifully", the verb *sang* is best described as

options.text: intransitive, because it is followed by an adverb
transitive, because it is followed by the direct object *the anthem*
auxiliary, because it helps the adverb *beautifully*

questions.explanation: Transitivity is decided by whether the verb has an object, not by whether an adverb appears later. "Sang what?" — the anthem. So *sang* is transitive, and *beautifully* is simply an adverb of manner attached to it. The same verb is intransitive in "The choir sang beautifully".

distractorRationale.a: The adverb is irrelevant; the presence of the object *the anthem* settles the matter
distractorRationale.c: Linking verbs join a subject to a describing word, and *beautifully* describes the singing, not the choir
distractorRationale.d: Auxiliaries help main verbs, never adverbs

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "Our class teacher ______ the corrected scripts to school yesterday."
questions.explanation: *Bring* is irregular and its simple past is *brought*. The time expression *yesterday* names a finished moment in the past, which is exactly what the simple past tense is for.

distractorRationale.a: Applies the regular -ed ending to an irregular verb
distractorRationale.b: Copies the sing/sang pattern, which does not apply to *bring*
distractorRationale.d: The present perfect cannot be used with a finished time expression such as *yesterday*

questions.stem: A linking verb can take a direct object.
questions.explanation: False. A linking verb expresses no action, so there is nothing for an object to receive. What follows a linking verb is a complement that describes or renames the subject, as in "She is a **nurse**" or "The soup tastes **peppery**".

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "The government has once again ______ the pump price of petrol."
questions.explanation: *Raise* (raise, raised, raised) is transitive: somebody raises something. Since the government acts on an object, *the pump price*, the transitive verb is required, and after *has* the participle is *raised*. *Rise* (rise, rose, risen) is intransitive — a price rises by itself, with no doer.

distractorRationale.a: *Risen* belongs to intransitive *rise* and cannot take the object *the pump price*
distractorRationale.b: *Rose* is both intransitive and a simple past form, so it cannot follow *has*
distractorRationale.d: *Arisen* comes from *arise*, which means to come into being, as in 'a problem has arisen'

questions.stem: In the sentence "Mrs Bello runs a thriving boutique in Ikeja", the verb *runs* is
questions.explanation: Here *runs* means 'manages', and it acts on the object *a thriving boutique*, so it is a transitive action verb. Many verbs switch between transitive and intransitive with a change of meaning: *runs* is intransitive in "She runs every morning", where nothing receives the action.

distractorRationale.a: Ignores the direct object *a thriving boutique*; this label would fit "She runs every morning"
distractorRationale.c: A linking verb would be followed by a word describing Mrs Bello, not by something she manages
distractorRationale.d: There is no second verb for *runs* to help
